title: OpenClaw alternatives for non-technical people (November 2026)
h1: openclaw alternatives for people who'd rather not run a server
description: Hermes Agent, Genspark Claw, Poke and Dusk Bot next to OpenClaw: setup, where it runs, which AI it uses, price and security, each with a dated source.
answer: if you like openclaw's idea, an assistant you text that works on your behalf, but not the setup and upkeep, there are three kinds of alternative: another open-source agent you still run yourself (hermes agent), a hosted assistant you just text (poke, genspark claw), or an app with a team of bots that can move to a hosted computer later (dusk bot). which fits depends on whether you want to keep your own ai sign-in and how much you want to look after.

method: we read each product's own homepage, docs and pricing page on 12 november 2026 and wrote down only what they say. for openclaw's security record we counted its published advisories through github's api the same day; the malicious-skills finding is from a security firm's audit as reported by the hacker news. we did not run the same tasks through every product, so this page compares what each offers, not how well each one does a job. we make dusk bot, so read our column with that in mind, and tell us at hello@dusk.bot if any cell is wrong.

sections.h: why people look for an openclaw alternative
sections.md:
openclaw is the best-known open-source assistant of its kind, and it's free. people who move on usually give one of three reasons.

**the upkeep.** its main install paths use a terminal and node.js, and it runs as a gateway on your machine or a server you look after. the desktop apps make the start easier, but updates and the server are still yours. openclaw itself apologised for a run of broken releases in late april 2026.[^16]

**security.** an agent that can read your mail and run commands is only as safe as its permissions and its add-ons. openclaw's github lists 722 published security advisories since january 2026, 14 of them critical,[^4] and an audit found 341 malicious skills in its skill store in february.[^15] the project has since added skill scanning and an outside audit, per its blog.

**the ai sign-in.** openclaw can reuse some vendor sign-ins, and its own docs recommend api keys for anthropic in production.[^3] what a vendor allows in third-party tools has changed during 2026, so check your ai provider's current terms whichever tool you pick.

**another agent you run yourself.** [hermes agent](/alternatives/hermes-agent) is the closest swap: also open source, also texted from chat apps, also yours to install and look after. it has a desktop app for mac and windows.

**a hosted assistant you just text.** poke and genspark claw need nothing installed. you text them from apps you already use. the ai is part of their plan, paid in their credits or tiers, rather than an ai account you already have.

**an app with a team of bots.** dusk bot is a desktop app where you keep a few bots, each with one job, its own memory and the ai you picked for it. they start on your own computer for free and can move to [dusk cloud](/docs/dusk-cloud), a computer we host, when you want them working with your laptop shut.

there is no importer from openclaw to dusk bot. the parts that move by hand are small: write each job you gave openclaw as a bot's job in plain words, connect the same apps once in **Connected apps**, and ask each bot for the routines you had ("every weekday at 8, summarise my inbox"). your notes about how you like things done are worth pasting into a bot's first message; it keeps them in its memory.

faq.a: not from the openclaw project, whose site says it has no hosted tier. some hosting companies sell managed openclaw; see [openclaw hosting](/alternatives/openclaw-hosting).

faq.q: what's the easiest openclaw alternative for a non-technical person?
faq.a: the hosted ones you just text (poke, genspark claw) have the least setup. dusk bot is an app you download and sign in to, with no terminal, and it keeps using the ai you already sign in to.
no. its creator joined openai in february 2026 and the project moved to the openclaw foundation, an independent non-profit announced in july 2026.
